{{Use dmy dates|date=April 2022}}
'''Thomas Baxter''' ({{floruit}} 1732–1740), was a schoolmaster and mathematician who published an erroneous method of [[squaring the circle]]. He was derided as a "pseudo-mathematician" by [[F. Y. Edgeworth]], writing for the ''[[Dictionary of National Biography]]''.<ref name=dnb>{{cite DNB |last=Edgeworth |first=F. Y. |wstitle=Baxter, Thomas (fl.1732) |volume=3 }}</ref>

When he was master of a private school at [[Crathorne, North Yorkshire]],<ref name=odnb>{{cite ODNB |last=McConnell |first=Anita |title=Baxter, Thomas (fl.1732) |date=2004 |id=1737 }}</ref> Baxter composed a book entitled ''The Circle squared'' (London: 1732), published in [[octavo]].<ref name=morgan/> The mathematical book begins with the untrue assertion that "if the [[diameter]] of a [[circle]] be unity or one, the [[circumference]] of that circle will be 3.0625", where the value should correctly be [[pi]].<ref name=dnb/> From this incorrect assumption, Baxter proves fourteen geometric theorems on circles, alongside some others on [[cone (geometry)|cones]] and [[ellipse]]s, which Edgeworth refers to as of "equal absurdity" to Baxter's other assertions.<ref name=dnb/> [[Thomas Gent]], who published the work, wrote in his reminisces, in ''The Life of Mr. Thomas Gent'', that "as it never proved of any effect, it was converted to waste paper, to the great mortification of the author".<ref>{{cite book |date=1832 |last=Gent |first=Thomas |title= The life of Mr. Thomas Gent |location=London |publisher=Thomas Thorpe |url=https://archive.org/details/lifeofmrthomasge00gentiala/page/182}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |title=Notes and Queries, 3rd Series, Vol. 5 |year=1849 |url=https://archive.org/details/s3notesqueries05londuoft/page/258 |page=258 }}</ref>

This book has received harsh reviews from modern mathematicians and scholars. Antiquary [[Edward Peacock (antiquary)|Edward Peacock]] referred to it as "no doubt, great rubbish".<ref>{{cite book |title=Notes and Queries, 3rd Series, Vol. 5 |year=1849 |url=https://archive.org/details/s3notesqueries05londuoft/page/348 |page=348 }}</ref> Mathematician [[Augustus De Morgan]] included Baxter's proof among his ''Budget of Paradoxes'' (1872), dismissing it as an absurd work.<ref name=morgan>{{cite book |first=Augustus |last=De Morgan |title=A Budget of Paradoxes |date=1872 |location=London |publisher=Longmans, Green, & Co. |page=87 |url=https://archive.org/details/cu31924092900863/page/n161 }}</ref> 

Baxter published another work, ''Matho, or the Principles of Astronomy and Natural Philosophy accommodated to the Use of Younger Persons'' (London: 1740). Unlike Baxter's other work, this volume enjoyed considerable popularity in its time.<ref>{{cite encyclopedia |last=Rose |first=Rev. Hugh James |title=Baxter, Thomas |encyclopedia=A New General Biographical Dictionary |volume=3 |date=1841 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=lCdMAAAAYAAJ |page=391 }}</ref><ref>{{cite encyclopedia |title=Baxter, Thomas |encyclopedia=A Critical Dictionary of English Literature and British and American Authors |volume=1 |date=1871 |last=Allibone |first=S. Austin |page=143 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=1eoaAQAAMAAJ }}</ref>
